story_text.value:
We started Mallard to make it easier to share our agent sessions and build things together. We spend much of our working day talking to Claude and Codex. Those conversations include the ideas, designs, and decisions behind our work. However they often stay on one machine, without backups or an easy way to share them.

3 months. 10 accounts on 20× plans. 100 billion tokens later, Mallard finally hatched.

Share and back up agent sessions using Cloudflare R2, Dropbox, or Mallard Cloud.

Explore the discussions and design decisions behind PRs, including Mallard’s hatching logs.

Pull and resume sessions in Codex or Claude Code with the original context.

For teams, Anthropic internally uses cloud VMs and Claude Tag so that teammates can work in shared agent conversations and pick up where others left off. Mallard lets teams achieve the same goal at almost zero cost, without any cloud VMs.

We want Mallard to be free and easy to use for everyone, rich or poor.

We built a lightweight version of GIT and reworked our storage protocol, removing CAS so Mallard can work with any cloud storage that supports LIST and PUT APIs. Bring your own storage or use Mallard Cloud. No Git server or expensive sandbox required.

We also added one-click sign-in for Dropbox and Cloudflare R2, so anyone can connect their own cloud storage to Mallard in just a few clicks.

We don’t think the internet, recommendation algorithms, or AI should be in the hands of just a few people. We hope Mallard helps more people share their work, find an audience, and have their voices heard.

Free and MIT licensed. Available on macOS and Windows. Website: https://mallard-ai.com/ GitHub: https://github.com/Git4Agent/mallard-app

story_text.value:
I run the *arr stack on my NAS and like the lazy bad admin I was, didn't backup the configuration files / databases etc. and proceeded to have to set this all up again when my NAS died. Needless to say this sucked. So I got started on a project to ensure I didn't have to go through this again and make it as hands off as possible. I wanted something that would collect backups on a schedule and put them somewhere else, ready in the event the worst strikes again. Doing some scouring I couldn't find anything that addressed this in the manner and scope I was looking for.

Backuparr is a single Docker container with a web UI. You give it each app's URL and API key, choose where the backups go (a local folder, Google Drive, OneDrive or Dropbox, all through rclone), and set a schedule and how long to keep them. It currently supports Radarr, Sonarr, Lidarr, Whisparr, Prowlarr, Profilarr, Bazarr, Tdarr, SABnzbd, NZBGet, Tautulli, Jellyfin, Emby, Plex, Seerr, and LazyLibrarian.

If an app has a backup API, Backuparr uses it. Emby, Plex and Seerr don't have one, so it takes a SQLite online backup of their databases from a mounted folder. All of them except Profilarr can be restored from Backuparr itself, once the service container is re-deployed.

The closest existing tool I found was servarr-backup, which covers Radarr, Sonarr and Prowlarr and sends backups to S3. I wanted more apps and the destinations I actually use.

Limitations: the backup archives themselves aren't encrypted. Only Backuparr's own config (API keys and passwords) and rclone credentials are. Jellyfin, Emby, Plex and Seerr need their folders mounted into the container.

I built this with my coding companion du jour claude-code, along with full review, a lot of self testing, debugging, full lab synthetic tests and running it against my own stack. I’ve been using it for two months now and would love some additional feedback.

Docs: https://rsaturns.github.io/backuparr/ License: AGPLv3

story_text.value:
Hi HN, my name is Federico. I’m an Italian graphic designer and full stack developer.

In recent months, there has been a lot of talk about the "second brain" articles and YouTube videos; everyone is still discussing it, but I see a significant difference between that and what the concept of a second brain means to me.

For me, the concept of a "second brain" is about building a 100% private knowledge base which means not uploading my own files (containing sensitive data) to be processed via cloud-based inference.

I’ve seen many videos discussing how to "build your own second brain" using Claude Code and Obsidian. I’ve always wondered: why should I upload my personal files such as certificates, my children’s birth certificates, or other sensitive personal data—to a service like Claude, where I have no idea where those files end up or who might be reading them? Furthermore, why should I rely on a graph-based viewer like Obsidian, effectively making myself dependent on third parties, paid services, and software that I have to install directly onto my own device?

From that came the idea to develop Knemora, an open-source, local-first project that runs locally by leveraging local inference.

The challenge involved: - choosing a modular architecture - ensuring ease of use via a CLI and a web interface - avoiding the need for users to install third-party software on their own devices - enabling setup in just 2 CLI commands - ensuring suitability for both developers (tech-savvy users) and various private organisations (such as notary offices, dental practices, insurance companies, etc.).

So far knemora includes the following features: - local inference via llama.cpp (with built-in support for cross-platform operation) - ability to use "knemora-tested" models or custom models from Hugging Face; simply run the command `./knemora load --model hf:<Hugging Face model name>` - a chatbot agent that answers questions and searches through your knowledge base based on your natural-language queries - a knowledge agent built using Google’s ADK 2.0 (my agentic orchestrator) - portable knowledge, markdown files are linked following the "LLM WIKI" pattern (as proposed by Andrej Karpathy) - BM25-based retrieval (no vector database required) - original documents are preserved and marked as (immutable) - dataset analysis powered by Polars

Currently, it is available only for macOS with Apple Silicon chips, but it will soon be available for Windows and Linux as well.

Version v0.2.0, available today on GitHub, covers these additional features and improvements:

- conversation continuity - automatic language matching - gemma 4 joins the tested model registry - more curated models ahead - more control over chat - wiki / direct chat modes - fast / deep chat modes - stronger knowledge compilation

My goal is to make Knemora more stable, responsive, easier to use and keep moving toward a stable v1.0.0.

Thank you!

Watch the alpha demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kl5qNrWPOnY

Explore the project: https://knemora.space

Code and documentation: https://github.com/federicolaterra/knemora

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Will. There are a few tools like this already, and my main ask is whether people would be interested in the interface (screenshot in README).

I use ChatGPT on the web to prompt codex because there are separate usage limits. I also prompt Claude Code the same way. It has better searching capabilities.

I want to give the web chat the thread, and copy-pasting doesn't work. I sometimes want:

1. prompts + thinking summaries

2. full detail w/ command outputs + diffs + subagents

Codex and Claude in their harnesses also want this just as much as I do for web.

I built an app where I can copy to clipboard the entire thread or just the last n messages, and then paste that so the web gets the full context. Via a local MCP Claude can see this same information from codex and vice versa.

It works, but the interface app for web isn't packaged yet because I am working on lots of projects and need to prioritise time and tokens. It does work rn for your harness agents in the linkedin repo.

Free and Apache 2.0, the interface would be too if people wanted it, I just don't want to go through the effort if no-one would find it useful.

Please let me know!

P.S. I've been working on much more interesting applications of using interfaces to make the complexity of formally checked software and maths more legible, but that's out of scope, it's just why I'm rationing my attention rn.

Here's a 5 min intro to that: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MBmVMMogXTA

Thanks!

story_text.value:
My company is pretty paranoid about leaking IP to the frontier labs through prompts, so we've all been diligent about disabling data sharing in Codex/Claude Code/etc. But yesterday my coworkers and I noticed that the setting had been silently reenabled in Codex. None of us knowingly opted back in.

You can check your settings here: https://chatgpt.com/settings/data-controls. Look for "Improve the model for everyone".

Curious if this is an isolated issue or something more widespread.

EDIT: looks like this has been noted before https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49643556

EDIT: apparently you can also turn off data sharing here: https://privacy.openai.com/policies?modal=take-control

story_text.value:
Before Recursive Super Intelligence.. a lot of alpha can be squeezed by recursively improve humans.. Dont you think? That's the idea of Recursive Human Intelligence.

Practically: it is a desktop that reads Claude Code, Codex, Pi chats, groups them into patterns and gives you specific feedback: touching habits that cost you time.

It is bring-your-own LLM; in terms of data privacy it is operating on things you already shared with LLMs.

I have gotten some good feedback myself already: on how I wrongly prompt sometimes, so it suggested a course I can take will and a book on MLOps to fill some gaps I miss.

I hope it does the same for you! Feel free to contribute :>

story_text.value:
This was my first experiment with AI assisted coding.

Backstory: I had a bunch of scripts to block sites on my work machines by redirecting them 127.0.0.1 etc. and they sort of worked. I needed something more serious and tried to get some commercial applications but there was nothing that really worked the way I wanted to (especially not on Linux). In Oct 2025 or so, I picked up aider and started building this out. Halfway through, I switched to Claude Code and used this as a vehicle to learn how to use assistants.

It blocks sites and apps on a schedule, and takes away your sudo during the hours you choose so you can’t just turn it off. I added several features like tracking usage, giving recommendations etc. and It's been actually very useful for me hence I decided to open source and productize it. Have a few users so far too.

It's been a nice learning experience for me. Not just for the implementation but also about the launch and marketing all assisted by AI.

Really looking forward to feedback from the folks here.

story_text.value:
I saw HackerTube (https://hackertube.org/) a few days ago, the YouTube videos HN keeps recommending, pulled from 19 years of comments. It made me want to flip through them instead of picking, so I built a TV for it. I have Algo fatigue.

Each topic area is a channel (DEVTV, SOLDER, RETRO, ORBIT, ...), plus HN Prime (the top 400), a music channel, and Late Night on ch 99, which only broadcasts 11pm-5am your local time and shows color bars otherwise.

Similar to HackerTube it was built with Claude Code in a few hours.

All credit for the data goes to HackerTube. Happy to hear channel ideas.
